questions.question: Q: What are Alvarado's four categories of racial representation?
questions.correctAnswer: Alvarado identified four common ways ethnic minorities are represented: exotic (fascinating, different, 'other'), pitied (needing help, impoverished), humorous (comic relief, stereotyped for laughs), and dangerous (threatening, criminal, terrorist). These categories are reductive and persist in contemporary media.

questions.question: Q: Why is diversity behind the camera important for representation?
questions.correctAnswer: When ethnic minorities are involved in writing, directing, and producing, representations tend to be more authentic and complex. White creators may unintentionally draw on stereotypes or miss cultural nuances. Diverse production teams bring lived experience that enriches characterisation and storytelling.

questions.question: Q: Evaluate whether ethnic representation in media is improving.
questions.correctAnswer: Representation has improved: more ethnic minority leads, successful diverse films (Black Panther), and social media enabling self-representation. However, progress is slow: the Annenberg Inclusion Initiative consistently finds underrepresentation, tokenism persists, and ethnic minorities remain excluded from senior production roles. Improvement is real but insufficient.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response Analyse how ethnicity is represented in one of your CSPs. [12 marks] <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: The representation of ethnicity in media products is shaped by the institutional context, target audience, and cultural moment of production. In many contemporary CSPs, ethnic minority representation has improved from historical stereotyping. Producers increasingly recognise that diverse audiences want to see themselves reflected in media, and that authentic representation is commercially viable. However, the quality of representation varies. Applying Alvarado's categories reveals that some representations still fall into reductive patterns: the 'exotic' other, the 'dangerous' threat, or the 'humorous' sidekick. These stereotypes persist because they serve familiar narrative functions and align with some audience expectations. More progressive representations show ethnic minority characters as complex, multi-dimensional individuals whose ethnicity is part of — but not the entirety of — their identity. This avoids the trap of reducing characters to their race while acknowledging the cultural specificity of their experience. The institutional context matters. Public service broadcasters have diversity obligations that commercial producers may not. Streaming platforms, seeking global audiences, often commission more diverse content than traditional broadcasters. Behind-the-camera diversity is crucial. When ethnic minority creators control the narrative, representations tend to be more authentic and nuanced. The contrast between externally created and self-authored representation
